quests.conceptTitle: Present Perfect: Have/Has + Past Participle
quests.faultySentence: I have saw that movie three times already.
quests.correctedSentence: I have seen that movie three times already.
quests.ruleExplanation: The present perfect is formed with 'have/has' plus the past participle, so the sentence needs 'have seen', not the simple past form 'saw'.
quests.nativeTip: The present perfect needs the past participle, not the simple past form — what is the participle of 'see'?

quests.conceptTitle: Present Perfect: Have/Has + Past Participle
quests.faultySentence: She has visit the new museum downtown.
quests.correctedSentence: She has visited the new museum downtown.
quests.ruleExplanation: Regular verbs form the past participle with '-ed', so the sentence needs 'has visited', not the base form 'has visit'.
quests.nativeTip: After 'has', the verb needs its past participle form — what ending does a regular verb take?

quests.conceptTitle: Present Perfect: Subject-Verb Agreement with Have/Has
quests.faultySentence: The committee have finished reviewing all the applications.
quests.correctedSentence: The committee has finished reviewing all the applications.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'The committee' functions as a singular subject here, so the present perfect needs 'has finished', not 'have finished'.
quests.nativeTip: 'The committee' is treated as a single unit here — does it take 'have' or 'has'?

quests.conceptTitle: Present Perfect: Experience Up to Now
quests.faultySentence: I lived in three different countries so far.
quests.correctedSentence: I have lived in three different countries so far.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'So far' signals an experience continuing to matter up to the present moment, so the sentence needs the present perfect 'have lived', not the simple past.
quests.nativeTip: 'So far' suggests this experience continues to be relevant up to now — does that call for simple past or present perfect?

quests.conceptTitle: Simple Past: Completed Actions Before Another Past Event
quests.faultySentence: She has worked at three companies before she started her own business.
quests.correctedSentence: She worked at three companies before she started her own business.
quests.ruleExplanation: Since this working experience happened and finished before starting her own business, a completed past sequence, the sentence needs the simple past 'worked', not the present perfect.
quests.nativeTip: This experience is placed clearly before another finished past action — does that call for present perfect or simple past?

quests.conceptTitle: Present Perfect: Unfinished Time Periods
quests.faultySentence: This year, the company launched five new products, and sales are already up twelve percent.
quests.correctedSentence: This year, the company has launched five new products, and sales are already up twelve percent.
quests.ruleExplanation: Since 'this year' is an unfinished time period and 'already' connects the action to the present, the sentence needs the present perfect 'has launched', not the simple past.
quests.nativeTip: 'This year' is a period that hasn't ended yet, and 'already' points to a connection with now — does that call for simple past or present perfect?

quests.conceptTitle: Past Perfect: Earlier of Two Past Actions
quests.faultySentence: By the time the ambulance arrived, the patient already lost consciousness.
quests.correctedSentence: By the time the ambulance arrived, the patient had already lost consciousness.
quests.correctedPart: the patient had already lost consciousness
quests.ruleExplanation: Since losing consciousness happened before the ambulance arrived, the earlier action needs the past perfect: 'had already lost consciousness'.
quests.nativeTip: Two past events are being compared — which happened first, the ambulance arriving or the loss of consciousness?

quests.conceptTitle: Past Perfect: Earlier of Two Past Actions
quests.faultySentence: She realized she forgot her passport only after boarding the plane.
quests.correctedSentence: She realized she had forgotten her passport only after boarding the plane.
quests.ruleExplanation: Since forgetting the passport happened before the moment of realization, it needs the past perfect: 'had forgotten', not the simple past.
quests.nativeTip: Which happened first — forgetting the passport, or realizing it after boarding?

quests.conceptTitle: Past Perfect: Earlier of Two Past Actions
quests.faultySentence: The investors were hesitant because the company missed its targets twice in the previous year.
quests.correctedSentence: The investors were hesitant because the company had missed its targets twice in the previous year.
quests.correctedPart: the company had missed its targets
quests.ruleExplanation: Since missing the targets happened before the investors' hesitation, the earlier event needs the past perfect: 'had missed'.
quests.nativeTip: Which came first — the investors' hesitation, or the missed targets from the previous year?

quests.conceptTitle: Past Perfect vs Simple Past: Sequencing Past Events
quests.faultySentence: When the fire alarm went off, everyone already left the building.
quests.correctedSentence: When the fire alarm went off, everyone had already left the building.
quests.ruleExplanation: Since people left before the alarm went off, the earlier action needs the past perfect: 'had already left', not the simple past.
quests.nativeTip: Two past events are compared — did people leave before or after the alarm went off?

quests.conceptTitle: Past Perfect vs Simple Past: Sequencing Past Events
quests.faultySentence: He was exhausted at the meeting because he worked through the night.
quests.correctedSentence: He was exhausted at the meeting because he had worked through the night.
quests.correctedPart: he had worked through the night
quests.ruleExplanation: Since working through the night happened before the meeting, the earlier action needs the past perfect: 'had worked through the night'.
quests.nativeTip: Which happened first — working through the night, or feeling exhausted at the meeting?

quests.conceptTitle: Past Perfect vs Simple Past: Sequencing Past Events
quests.faultySentence: The audience applauded enthusiastically; the performance exceeded everyone's expectations.
quests.correctedSentence: The audience applauded enthusiastically; the performance had exceeded everyone's expectations.
quests.correctedPart: the performance had exceeded everyone's expectations
quests.ruleExplanation: Since the performance exceeded expectations before the applause, the earlier action needs the past perfect: 'had exceeded'.
quests.nativeTip: Which happened first — the performance exceeding expectations, or the audience applauding?

quests.conceptTitle: Future: Present Continuous for Fixed Arrangements
quests.faultySentence: I will meet my accountant tomorrow at ten; it's already on my calendar.
quests.correctedSentence: I am meeting my accountant tomorrow at ten; it's already on my calendar.
quests.ruleExplanation: Since the appointment is already fixed and confirmed, the present continuous 'am meeting' fits better than 'will meet', which suggests a spontaneous decision.
quests.nativeTip: The context mentions this is already scheduled on a calendar — does that call for 'will' or the present continuous?

quests.conceptTitle: Future: Going To for Predictions Based on Evidence
quests.faultySentence: Look at the smoke coming from the engine — the car will break down soon.
quests.correctedSentence: Look at the smoke coming from the engine — the car is going to break down soon.
quests.correctedPart: the car is going to break down
quests.ruleExplanation: Predictions based on present evidence use 'going to', so the sentence needs 'is going to break down', not 'will break down'.
quests.nativeTip: This prediction is based on visible evidence right now, the smoke — does that call for 'will' or 'going to'?

quests.conceptTitle: Future: Will for Spontaneous Decisions
quests.faultySentence: I can't decide what to order — actually, I am going to have the soup.
quests.correctedSentence: I can't decide what to order — actually, I will have the soup.
quests.ruleExplanation: Spontaneous decisions made at the moment of speaking use 'will', so the sentence needs 'I will have', not 'I am going to have'.
quests.nativeTip: This decision is being made right at the moment of speaking, not planned earlier — does that call for 'going to' or 'will'?

quests.conceptTitle: Present Perfect Continuous: Emphasizing Duration
quests.faultySentence: I have wrote this report for the last three hours.
quests.correctedSentence: I have been writing this report for the last three hours.
quests.ruleExplanation: When emphasizing the duration of an ongoing action, the present perfect continuous is used: 'have been writing', not the incorrect form 'have wrote'.
quests.nativeTip: The phrase 'for the last three hours' emphasizes how long an ongoing action has continued — does that call for the simple or continuous perfect form?

quests.conceptTitle: Present Perfect Simple: Emphasizing Completed Result
quests.faultySentence: She has been reading five books this month.
quests.correctedSentence: She has read five books this month.
quests.ruleExplanation: When emphasizing a completed quantity or result, the present perfect simple is used: 'has read', not the continuous form 'has been reading'.
quests.nativeTip: The sentence emphasizes a completed number of books, a result, not an ongoing activity — does that call for the simple or continuous perfect form?

quests.conceptTitle: Present Perfect Continuous: Emphasizing Duration
quests.faultySentence: My eyes hurt because I have stared at this screen all afternoon.
quests.correctedSentence: My eyes hurt because I have been staring at this screen all afternoon.
quests.ruleExplanation: Since the sentence emphasizes a continuous activity leading to a present effect, the present perfect continuous is needed: 'have been staring'.
quests.nativeTip: The ongoing activity over the afternoon explains the current effect on your eyes — does that call for the simple or continuous perfect form?

quests.conceptTitle: Past Perfect Continuous: Duration Before Another Past Event
quests.faultySentence: Her legs ached because she had run for two hours before stopping to rest.
quests.correctedSentence: Her legs ached because she had been running for two hours before stopping to rest.
quests.ruleExplanation: Since the sentence emphasizes a continuous activity leading to a past effect, the past perfect continuous is needed: 'had been running'.
quests.nativeTip: This describes an ongoing activity leading to a past result, her aching legs — does that call for the simple or continuous past perfect form?

quests.conceptTitle: Past Perfect Continuous: Duration Before Another Past Event
quests.faultySentence: By the time help arrived, the crew had repaired the engine for six hours, though the damage remained unfixed.
quests.correctedSentence: By the time help arrived, the crew had been repairing the engine for six hours, though the damage remained unfixed.
quests.ruleExplanation: Since the repair was still ongoing and unfinished, the past perfect continuous is needed: 'had been repairing', not the completed form 'had repaired'.
quests.nativeTip: The sentence explains the damage remained unfixed — does that fit a completed action or an ongoing one?

quests.conceptTitle: Past Perfect Continuous: Duration Before Another Past Event
quests.faultySentence: The students were tired because they had studied for the entrance exam for months without a break.
quests.correctedSentence: The students were tired because they had been studying for the entrance exam for months without a break.
quests.ruleExplanation: Since the sentence emphasizes a continuous activity over an extended period leading to a past effect, the past perfect continuous is needed: 'had been studying'.
quests.nativeTip: This describes an ongoing activity over months leading to a past result, their tiredness — does that call for the simple or continuous past perfect form?

quests.conceptTitle: Duration: For with a Length of Time
quests.faultySentence: I have known her since ten years.
quests.correctedSentence: I have known her for ten years.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'For' is used with a length of time, while 'since' is used with a starting point, so the sentence needs 'for ten years'.
quests.nativeTip: 'Ten years' is a length of time, not a starting point — which word fits a duration?

quests.conceptTitle: Duration: Since with a Starting Point
quests.faultySentence: The factory has been closed for the pandemic began.
quests.correctedSentence: The factory has been closed since the pandemic began.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Since' introduces a specific starting point, especially a clause like 'the pandemic began', so the sentence needs 'since the pandemic began'.
quests.nativeTip: This describes a specific starting event, not a length of time — which word fits a starting point?

quests.conceptTitle: Past Perfect: Adverb Placement with Had
quests.faultySentence: By the time the review was complete, the team already had submitted three revisions.
quests.correctedSentence: By the time the review was complete, the team had already submitted three revisions.
quests.ruleExplanation: The adverb 'already' typically comes right after the auxiliary 'had', so the sentence needs 'had already submitted', not 'already had submitted'.
quests.nativeTip: Adverbs like 'already' usually go directly after the auxiliary verb, not before it — where should 'already' be placed?

quests.conceptTitle: Tense Sequence: Past Perfect for Background Events in Narrative
quests.faultySentence: The negotiations continued for months before the two companies finally signed the agreement, ending a process that begins with a simple phone call.
quests.incorrectPart: a process that begins with a simple phone call
quests.correctedSentence: The negotiations continued for months before the two companies finally signed the agreement, ending a process that had begun with a simple phone call.
quests.correctedPart: a process that had begun with a simple phone call
quests.ruleExplanation: Since this describes the origin of the process, earlier than the main narrated events, the past perfect is needed: 'had begun', not the present tense 'begins'.
quests.nativeTip: This clause describes how the whole process originally started, before the events described earlier in the sentence — what tense fits background information further in the past?

quests.conceptTitle: Tense Sequence: Matching Past Tense for Specific Past Findings
quests.faultySentence: The scientist explained that the initial results are inconclusive due to a testing error last spring.
quests.correctedSentence: The scientist explained that the initial results were inconclusive due to a testing error last spring.
quests.ruleExplanation: Since this refers to a specific past finding rather than a timeless truth, the tense should match the past reporting verb: 'were inconclusive', not 'are inconclusive'.
quests.nativeTip: This describes a specific finding tied to a testing error last spring, not a timeless fact — does it need to stay in the present or shift to match the past reporting?

quests.conceptTitle: Tense Sequence: Past Perfect for Events Prior to the Main Past Action
quests.faultySentence: By the end of the trial, the defendant's lawyer proved that his client never leaves the city that weekend.
quests.incorrectPart: his client never leaves the city
quests.correctedSentence: By the end of the trial, the defendant's lawyer proved that his client had never left the city that weekend.
quests.correctedPart: his client had never left the city
quests.ruleExplanation: Since the client's whereabouts refer to a specific past weekend, prior to the trial's conclusion, the past perfect is needed: 'had never left', not the present tense 'never leaves'.
quests.nativeTip: The proof relates to something true during that specific weekend, before the trial's conclusion — what tense fits an event further back in the past?

quests.conceptTitle: Present Perfect: Have/Has + Past Participle
quests.faultySentence: I have finish reading that novel you recommended.
quests.correctedSentence: I have finished reading that novel you recommended.
quests.ruleExplanation: Regular verbs form the past participle with '-ed', so the sentence needs 'have finished', not the base form 'have finish'.
quests.nativeTip: After 'have', the verb needs its past participle form — what ending does a regular verb take?

quests.conceptTitle: Past Perfect: Earlier of Two Past Actions
quests.faultySentence: The inspectors realized the bridge design contained a flaw that engineers overlook during the initial review.
quests.incorrectPart: engineers overlook during the initial review
quests.correctedSentence: The inspectors realized the bridge design contained a flaw that engineers had overlooked during the initial review.
quests.correctedPart: engineers had overlooked during the initial review
quests.ruleExplanation: Since overlooking the flaw happened before the later realization, the earlier action needs the past perfect: 'had overlooked'.

quests.conceptTitle: Past Perfect Continuous: Duration Before Another Past Event

quests.correctedSentence: Her hands trembled because she had been waiting for the results all morning.
quests.ruleExplanation: Since the sentence emphasizes a continuous activity leading to a past effect, the past perfect continuous is needed: 'had been waiting'.
